# Results — Study 444 (Dow Theory)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **a
primary trend is only valid when the Industrials and the Transports confirm each other (both
making higher highs); stay out when they disagree** — encoded as a mechanical rule and traded
against buy-and-hold. We be **long the Industrials only while the confirmation regime is on**
and in **cash** otherwise, with one execution lag and realistic costs. Offline & deterministic
once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance auto-adjusted daily closes — Industrials = **DIA**, Transports = **IYT** (tradable ETF proxies, public, no key) |
| Window | 2004-01-02 → 2026-05-29 (**22.4** years; 5,637 trading days) |
| As-of | **2026-05-31** (last full calendar month before the build; no partial period) |
| Fingerprint | `1ee3a36320fb` (ETF panel) · `ea24513f67a9` (long index panel) |
| Confirmation rule | both averages close at/above their **63-day trailing high** → trend *confirmed* (latched ON until both close below their 63-day trailing **low** → OFF) |
| Trade / lag / costs | long the Industrials when confirmed, else cash; signal at close *t*, return earned *t+1* (one lag); **2 bps** one-way per flip; cash earns 0 (excess-vs-excess) |
| Robustness tape | ^DJI / ^DJT **price-only** index levels, 1992-01-02 → 2026-05-29 (34 years) |

> **Price-only vs total-return (named).** DIA/IYT are auto-adjusted (≈ total return), so the
> headline race is total-return vs total-return. The long robustness tape (^DJI/^DJT) is
> **price-only** (no dividends) and is used only to confirm the *sign and significance* of the
> active spread over a longer history, never for level comparisons.

## The race — does timing the trend with the Transports beat just holding?

Buy-and-hold the Industrials vs the Dow-Theory-timed book (long only when confirmed, else cash).
Both legs are excess-of-cash (cash earns 0). The decisive number is the **HAC (Newey-West)
one-sample t** on the *active daily spread* (net strategy − benchmark): if confirmation adds
timing value, it must clear **t ≥ 2** here.

| mode | on-fraction | CAGR | Sharpe | max DD | active/yr | active HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **buy & hold** | — | **+9.75%** | **0.612** | −51.9% | — | — |
| latched regime | 62.4% | +5.56% | 0.599 | −22.5% | **−4.99%** | **−1.94** |
| instantaneous flag | 5.5% | +0.69% | 0.351 | −8.4% | **−10.18%** | **−3.14** |

Read it carefully. Timing the trend with the confirmation rule **does not add value** — the
active spread is **negative** at every setting, and its HAC *t* is **−1.94** (latched) / **−3.14**
(instantaneous): if anything, confirmation timing *significantly underperforms* buy-and-hold.
The latched book matches buy-and-hold's **Sharpe** (0.599 vs 0.612) only because it spends 38%
of the time in cash, which halves the drawdown (−22.5% vs −51.9%) — but it gives up **4.2
points of CAGR** to do it. That lower drawdown is plain de-risking (less time in the market),
not a confirmation edge: you would get the same trade-off from any rule that sat in cash a
third of the time.

## Content test — is the confirmation flag actually predictive?

Strip out the cash-drag and ask the clean question: is the Industrials' **next-day** return
higher on confirmed days than on non-confirmed days?

| regime | confirmed days | non-confirmed days | spread/yr | Welch *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| latched | +9.51%/yr | +13.17%/yr | **−3.67%** | **−0.41** |
| instantaneous flag | +19.20%/yr | +10.40%/yr | +8.80% | **+1.01** |

On the latched regime, confirmed days actually return **less** than non-confirmed days (spread
−3.67%/yr). The instantaneous flag is positive (+8.80%/yr) but **does not clear t = 2** (Welch
*t* = 1.01) — and it fires only 5.5% of the time, so it is statistically and operationally
empty. There is no reliable forward edge in the confirmation.

## Placebo — is it the Transports, or just being in cash a third of the time?

Replace the real confirmation regime with a **random** 0/1 regime matched to the same
**on-fraction** and average **run length** (a two-state Markov chain), re-run the identical
backtest, and ask how often a random regime's net Sharpe **beats** the real one.

| | observed net Sharpe | placebo mean | p(random ≥ real) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| latched regime | 0.599 | 0.489 | **0.197** |

A random cash-timing regime with the same persistence beats the real Dow-Theory regime **~20%
of the time**. The real regime is modestly *above* the random average — but that lift comes
from *how often* it sits in cash (and that cash happened to dodge the 2008/2020 crashes in this
one sample), not from the Industrials/Transports *agreement* carrying information. p = 0.197 is
nowhere near significant.

## Robustness — negative at every knob

| | active/yr | active HAC *t* | Strat Sharpe vs BH 0.612 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 bps (gross) | −4.96% | −1.92 | 0.602 |
| 2 bps | −4.99% | −1.94 | 0.599 |
| 10 bps | −5.12% | −1.98 | 0.585 |
| lookback 21 | — | **−2.70** | 0.367 |
| lookback 63 | — | −1.94 | 0.599 |
| lookback 200 | — | −2.31 | 0.507 |
| **^DJI/^DJT 1992→2026 (34y, latched)** | −4.08% | **−1.97** | 0.543 vs 0.552 |

The active spread is negative across costs and across every trailing-high window (21–200 days),
and the sign and significance hold on the independent 34-year price-only index history (active
*t* = −1.97; content spread −1.28%/yr, Welch *t* = −0.19). Costs are not the story — there was
no gross edge to charge against.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful

On a deterministic two-series panel where we **plant** a confirmation edge (the Industrials'
return is genuinely boosted on confirmed days), the content test behaves exactly as it must:

| planted edge | confirmed-day fraction | confirmed/yr | non/yr | spread/yr | Welch *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.000** (no edge) | 2.9% | +16.22% | +5.57% | +10.65% | **+0.50** |
| **+0.003/day** (large planted) | 3.2% | +97.24% | +5.69% | +91.55% | **+4.54** |

With **no** planted edge the test sits at *t* ≈ 0.5 (it does not manufacture significance from
noise); a large planted edge lights up to *t* = 4.54. The harness *can* detect a real
confirmation effect — it simply doesn't find one on the real tape. (A synthetic control is a
machinery proof, never market evidence.)

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** No test clears the desk's **t ≥ 2** bar in the believers' direction. The
  active spread vs buy-and-hold is **negative** (HAC *t* = −1.94 latched, −3.14 instantaneous);
  the direct content test of confirmed-vs-non-confirmed next-day returns is **−3.67%/yr (t =
  −0.41)** latched and **+8.80%/yr but only t = 1.01** on the flag; the result is unchanged in
  sign and significance over 34 years of index history. Indistinguishable from noise (and if
  anything pointed the wrong way).
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The only thing the rule "buys" you is a smaller drawdown (−22.5%
  vs −51.9%), and that is pure de-risking — it spends 38% of the time in cash and surrenders
  **4.2 points of CAGR** for a Sharpe that is *no better* than buy-and-hold (0.599 vs 0.612).
  There is no residual edge to deploy; the apparent "downside protection" is just less market
  exposure, available from any cash-timing rule.
- **Does the confirmation actually work? — BUSTED.** A **random** regime with the same
  on-fraction and persistence beats the real Industrials/Transports confirmation regime ~20%
  of the time (placebo p = 0.197). The famous "the Transports must confirm the Industrials"
  signal carries no detectable information beyond *being in cash sometimes* — the agreement
  between the two averages is not what's doing the (modest, drawdown-only) work.
